introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography, Paper 3 (0750), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer ALL THE THREE QUESTIONS. Question ONE carries THIRTY-FOUR marks and the rest carry THIRTY-THREE marks each.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answer.

Calculators are allowed.

Materials required: Topographic map, Graph Paper and photograph.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) i) Describe the difficulties caused by the relief in the development of the eastern portion of the map area. **(4 marks)**

ii) Suggest any one measure to overcome the problems identified. **(2 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Difficulties caused by the relief in the east of the map (4 marks).** The eastern portion (roughly eastings 23 to 26) is a narrow built-up coastal plain that is quickly replaced by hills, valleys and wet low ground. Any four of the following, each with its evidence on the map (1 mark each):

1. *Steep slopes restrict building and the growth of the town.* The contour lines are very close together on the hill near Towe (about eastings 25 to 26, northings 92 to 93, contours rising from about 150 m to over 300 m) and on the rising ground north of Limbe Town. Land this steep is unsuitable for houses, factories and playgrounds, and building there needs expensive levelling, retaining walls and strong foundations, so the urban area cannot spread freely to the north-east.
2. *Road building is difficult and costly.* Roads must wind round hills and spurs or climb steep gradients, so the roads in the north-east (towards Kulu, Ross, Ebongo and Wututu) are few, long and winding, and many are only tracks. Transport is slow and expensive, so the north-east is poorly linked to the port and market of Limbe.
3. *Low, flat, badly drained ground near the coast and in the valleys.* Around Mawoh, Motowa and Morton Point the ground is low and partly swampy or covered by mangrove (swamp and mangrove symbols of the key). Such ground is liable to flooding at high tide and in the rainy season, and its soft soil needs costly drainage, filling and special foundations before building.
4. *Many streams in valleys cut the area into separate blocks.* The blue stream lines flowing from the hills towards the sea need bridges or culverts, which raises costs, and valleys with steep sides isolate villages from each other.
5. *Steep, bare or cleared slopes are exposed to erosion, gullies and landslides in the heavy rainfall of the Mount Cameroon region, and farming is possible only on the smaller, gentler patches; water, electricity and other services are difficult to supply to scattered houses on slopes.*

**(ii) One measure (2 marks).** Any one, stated (1) and explained (1):
- *Terracing and cut-and-fill with retaining walls* so that house plots and roads are made level on the slope and the soil is held;
- *Building roads along the contours with gentle gradients (zigzags, hairpin bends)* and with bridges and culverts across the streams, to link the hill areas to Limbe Town;
- *Draining and filling the swampy ground, or leaving it as a protected green belt,* and putting buildings on raised foundations;
- *Afforestation or tree-planting of the steep slopes* to prevent erosion and landslides and keep them out of building.

**Tip.** Name a place or a grid square of the map in every point; a general list of the problems of relief without map evidence loses marks.

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) i) Calculate the detour index of the road connecting Limbe Town at grid square 2390 to Bonjongo, besides spot height 600m. **(3 marks)**

ii) State the significance of your result. **(2 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Detour index (3 marks).** The detour index measures how far a road departs from the straight line between two places:

$$
\text{Detour index} = \frac{\text{actual road distance}}{\text{straight-line distance}}
$$

**Method (steps shown for 3 marks).**
1. *Locate the two places.* Limbe Town is in grid square 2390 (easting 23, northing 90: read the easting first, then the northing). Bonjongo is the village in the north-east of the map, at the end of the main road, next to the 600 m height (about easting 22, northing 96); it is not the "Lower" village further west.
2. *Measure the road distance.* Lay a thread (or the edge of a strip of paper marked at each bend) along the road: Limbe Town, the junction on the coast road, Mukunda village, then north to Bonjongo. Straighten the thread and convert its length with the scale (on this reduced reproduction count the 1 km grid squares instead of using the printed bar; on the full-size map 2 cm = 1 km).
3. *Measure the straight-line distance* between the two points with a ruler and convert it in the same way.
4. *Divide* the road distance by the straight-line distance (no unit, because the two distances are in the same unit).

**Result obtained on the map (approximate reading, to be checked on the original).** Road distance about 7.5 km; straight-line distance about 5.7 km:

$$
\text{Detour index} = \frac{7.5\ \text{km}}{5.7\ \text{km}} \approx 1.3
$$

Any answer between about 1.2 and 1.4 is accepted when the two distances are shown, because the measure depends on the exact points chosen and on the thread. The value can never be less than 1.

**(ii) Significance (2 marks).**
- A value of 1 would mean a perfectly straight road. A value of about 1.3 means that the road is about 30 % longer than the straight line, so it is moderately winding (1 mark).
- The road bends because of the relief: it climbs the foothills of Mount Etinde (Mount Cameroon area), follows the gentler slopes and the ridge lines, and goes round the hills and valleys between Limbe Town, Mukunda and Bonjongo. The journey is therefore longer, slower and costlier (more fuel and time) than the straight distance suggests, which isolates the village and raises the cost of carrying farm produce to the market in Limbe (1 mark). A higher index would show a still more difficult relief; a value near 1 would show a flat land with a direct road.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) i) Which natural hazard is the coastline from the Oil Refinery to Ambas bay vulnerable to? Justify your answer using evidence from the map only. **(2 marks)**

ii) Suggest two measures to mitigate or reduce the negative impact of this hazard in the area. **(2 marks)**

d) i) Comment on two evidences on the map to show that Limbe occupies a strategic position for its rapid economic development. **(4 marks)**

ii) Draw a sketch map to show the main land uses on the map area. **(4 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Strategic position (4 marks, 2 per evidence: evidence 1 + comment 1).** Any two of the following:
1. *Coastal location with a port and an industry linked to the sea.* Limbe stands on the Atlantic coast, on a bay (Ambas bay), and the map shows an anchor (seaport/wharf) symbol and a long jetty at the Oil Refinery, with boats in the bay. A sheltered sea outlet allows the import of equipment and the export of oil products and farm produce, fishing and industries, so it attracts investment and jobs and encourages growth.
2. *A dense network of roads converging on the town.* The coast road (a main road) enters Limbe Town from the west, another main road runs north to Mukunda village and Bonjongo, and others run north-east towards Kulu, Ross, Ebongo and Wututu. Limbe is a route centre (nodal point): it is easy to reach, so it is the market and service centre for the whole area.
3. *A rich agricultural hinterland.* Large areas of plantations (tree crops) and rural settlements surround the town (north, north-west and north-east). They supply labour, raw materials and food, and they use the services, banks and the market of Limbe (a major market symbol is shown in the east of the town).
4. *Tourism, administration and services.* The beaches and bays, the Botanical Garden and the Omnisport Stadium, together with schools, hospitals (H symbols) and a large built-up centre, show a town with many functions (administration, services, leisure), which draws visitors and people from other places.
5. *Space for expansion.* The urban area lies on a gently sloping coastal plain, and the map shows a "planned town extension" (hatched area near the stadium), so the town can grow in an orderly way.

**(ii) Sketch map of the main land uses (4 marks).**
1. Draw a frame; give a title (for example "Main land uses of the Limbe map area"), a north arrow and a scale (for example 1 square = 1 km, or a line scale) (1 mark).
2. Outline the coast and the sea, and draw the main roads (the coast road, the road to Mukunda and Bonjongo, the road to the north-east) as reference lines (1 mark).
3. Shade, with a different pattern or colour for each land use, in the right place (1.5 marks): urban settlement (Limbe Town and the strip along the coast to the west and the east); industrial area (Oil Refinery on the west coast); planned town extension and sporting ground (Omnisport Stadium); rural settlements (villages such as Mukunda, Bonjongo, Ebongo and Wututu); plantations or tree crops (north and north-east); evergreen forest (the Mount Etinde slopes in the north-west); scrub or savanna patches; beach and mangrove on the coast.
4. A complete key explaining each pattern, and the names of the main places (0.5 mark).

![fig-4](gce-al-geography-2026-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*Model sketch (schematic: positions are simplified from the map and are not drawn to exact scale).*

questions.enonce_markdown:
e) Study Figure 1 on a separate sheet inserted, which is a photograph of part of an urban area in Yaounde, and answer the questions that follow.

![fig-3](gce-al-geography-2026-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Figure 1: Partial view of an urban neighbourhood in Yaounde.*

i) Based on the nature of the buildings, suggest the type of urban problem depicted on the photograph. **(2 marks)**

ii) Describe TWO problems that are associated with these types of areas. **(4 marks)**

iii) Suggest TWO measures to tackle the urban problem. **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The urban problem (2 marks).** The photograph shows a **slum (an informal, spontaneous or unplanned settlement) with poor-quality, overcrowded housing and a congested street** (1 mark). Evidence (1 mark): the buildings are low, single-storey and very closely packed, with no regular layout; many are built of planks, mud bricks or mixed materials and are roofed with rusting corrugated iron sheets; the street is narrow and crowded with cars, traders' stalls and pedestrians; and rubbish (old tyres) lies on the ground.

**(ii) Two problems associated with these areas (4 marks, 2 each: the problem 1 + the explanation 1).** Any two:
1. *Poor sanitation and ill health.* There is little space for drains, toilets or refuse collection; water supply is poor and rubbish accumulates, so water-borne diseases (cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea) and malaria spread easily in the overcrowded houses.
2. *Fire, flood and landslide risk and poor access.* The houses are packed together, built of flammable materials and often linked to the electricity supply informally, so a fire spreads quickly; the narrow lanes are impassable for fire engines and ambulances. Many such quarters in hilly Yaounde are built on steep slopes or in swampy valley bottoms, where floods and landslides occur.
3. *Traffic congestion, noise and pollution.* A market street used by vehicles, traders and pedestrians at the same time is slow and dangerous, causing accidents, delays and air and noise pollution.
4. *Insecurity and social problems.* Overcrowding, unemployment and lack of street lighting encourage theft, aggression and delinquency; the people lack titles to their land, so they can be evicted and do not invest in their houses.
5. *Pressure on services.* Schools, health centres, water and electricity networks are insufficient for the number of people.

**(iii) Two measures to tackle the problem (5 marks, 2.5 each: measure 1 + development 1.5).** Any two:
1. *Upgrading the existing quarters:* the city council and the State bring in clean water, electricity, paved roads, drains, street lighting, public toilets and a regular refuse collection, and widen the main lanes for fire engines and ambulances, with the participation of the residents.
2. *Urban planning and control of land use:* prepare a master plan with zoning, mark out building plots with roads and services before houses are built, give secure land titles and enforce the building regulations (no building on steep slopes, river banks or swamps).
3. *Affordable and social housing:* build low-cost houses and give loans to low-income families (for example through housing finance institutions such as the Crédit Foncier du Cameroun), and move families living in danger zones to safer, serviced plots.
4. *Reducing the pressure on the capital:* develop jobs, services and infrastructure in the rural areas and in other towns (decentralisation) so that fewer migrants settle in Yaounde.
5. *Public education and community action* on hygiene, waste disposal and building standards; improvement of public transport and organisation of the market stalls to reduce congestion.
